newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices hold firm despite news of healthy stocks.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices hold firm despite news of healthy stocks.

text.p: Oil prices rose on Friday despite a report by the West's energy watchdog which showed that rich consumer nations emerged from the peak demand season with well stocked oil inventories.

April futures for world benchmark crude Brent Blend, under pressure since the start of the year, sagged during the afternoon session then staged a strong recovery to trade 22 cents higher at $19.92 a barrel by 1611 GMT.
Futures traders said that although long-term fundamentals were bearish, an unexpected drop in temperatures in the U.S. Northeast, the world's biggest heating oil market, was supportive short-term.
"A technical recovery aided by prospects of cooler weather in the U.S. Northeast is giving the complex a slightly healthier appearance in the short term," London brokers GNI said in a daily report.

The Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its monthly oil report for end February that rising crude oil supplies had allowed the oil industry to replenish lean stocks. These were higher than the previous year for the first time in 18 months.
In addition, world oil output from both OPEC and non-OPEC producers was set to outstrip strong growth in world demand, the IEA said.

Global oil output rose by 2.28 million barrels a day (bpd) in the past four months to 74.8 million bpd, the agency, which draws its membership from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), said.
"A substantial relaxation in global supply/demand fundamentals led to a steep decline in...crude oil prices," it added.

Low inventory stocks, a delay in anticipated additional crude oil from producers outside the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and Iraq's absence from oil markets until December 1996 helped to push oil prices to their highest in nearly six years last October.

But the resumption of Iraqi crude oil exports under the U.N. oil-for-food plan in December, a mild winter and continued quota busting by some OPEC members led to a 20 percent fall in prices since mid-January.

The IEA is forecasting growth of 1.9 million bpd in world oil demand this year to 73.7 million bpd. But it says countries outside OPEC will meet the extra volume, leaving no room on oil markets for rising OPEC output.

OPEC supplies, boosted by the second full month of Iraqi supplies under the U.N. oil-for-food plan, kept output at 26.98 million bpd in February, the IEA estimated. This is against an official OPEC ceiling of 25.03 million bpd.
A balanced market needed only 25.4 million bpd of OPEC supply on average this year, it said.

"We think the amount OPEC is producing at the moment is above average demand for the year but the outlook for the market isn't as bad as the IEA figures would suggest," said Mike Barry at Energy Market Consultants.
